etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Latin inhaerentem, accusative singular of inhaerēns, present active participle of inhaereō (“I am closely connected with; adhere to”).

definitions.definition: Naturally as part or consequence of something.

quote.citation: 1837, L[etitia] E[lizabeth] L[andon], Ethel Churchill: Or, The Two Brides. […], volume I, London: Henry Colburn, […], →OCLC, pages 244–245:
quote.text: There is a stern melancholy in his dark features, inherent and engrossing, which rivets the attention.

quote.citation: 2014 June 14, “It's a gas”, in The Economist, volume 411, number 8891:
quote.text: One of the hidden glories of Victorian engineering is proper drains. […] But out of sight is out of mind. And that, together with the inherent yuckiness of the subject, means that many old sewers have been neglected and are in dire need of repair.
